# Descriptive Analysis of Animal Health Conditions

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Create color palette for health conditions
custom_colors =
  c("#0868ac", "#43a2ca", "#7bccc4", "#bae4bc", "#f0f9e8")
```


### Health Conditions by Animal Class

```{r, fig.retina=2, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Count number of cases by animal class and health condition
health_by_class =
  park_ranger_new |>
    count(animal_class_new, animal_condition, name = "n")

# Order animal classes by total number of cases (descending)
class_order =
  health_by_class |>
    group_by(animal_class_new) |>
    summarise(total = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(total)) |>
    pull(animal_class_new)

# Apply the ordered factor levels to animal_class_new
health_by_class$animal_class_new =
  factor(
    health_by_class$animal_class_new,
    levels = class_order
  )

# Create stacked bar chart using plotly with custom colors and hover info
plot_ly(
    data  = health_by_class,
    x     = ~animal_class_new,
    y     = ~n,
    color = ~animal_condition,
    type  = "bar",
    colors = custom_colors,
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "Animal Class: ", health_by_class$animal_class_new, "<br>",
      "Health Condition: ", health_by_class$animal_condition, "<br>",
      "Count: ", health_by_class$n
    ),
    height = 600,
    width = 700
  ) |>
  layout(
    title  = "Health Conditions by Animal Class",
    xaxis  = list(title = "Animal Class"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Number of Cases"),
    barmode = "stack"
  )
```

Birds/Raptors have the highest overall number of reports, followed by Small Mammals and Large Mammals.  

However, once the data are split by health condition, several patterns deviate from this overall ranking:  

- Small Mammals show more Unknown, DOA, and Unhealthy cases than Birds/Raptors, despite having a lower total count.  
This may be because small mammals (like rats, hamsters, rabbits) are harder to observe when sick and often found only when severely ill or deceased.  

- Fish and Marine Mammals have extremely few reports overall, but their conditions tend to cluster (e.g., more DOA), likely due to rare sightings and the difficulty of detecting mild illness in aquatic species.  
  
- Reptiles/Amphibians form a small portion of total cases yet show a relatively higher share of Injured or DOA reports, possibly because people notice them mainly when something is visibly wrong. 
  
These differences suggest that how often an animal is reported—and why it is reported—depends heavily on visibility, human contact, and the ease of identifying distress across species.  

<br><br>

### Health Conditions by Borough

```{r, fig.retina=2, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Count number of cases by borough and health condition
health_by_borough =
  park_ranger_new |>
    count(borough, animal_condition, name = "n")

# Order boroughs by total number of cases (descending)
borough_order =
  health_by_borough |>
    group_by(borough) |>
    summarise(total = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(total)) |>
    pull(borough)

# Apply the ordered factor levels to borough
health_by_borough$borough =
  factor(
    health_by_borough$borough,
    levels = borough_order
  )

# Build clean hover text (fix the main issue)
health_by_borough$hover_text =
  paste0(
    "Borough: ", health_by_borough$borough, "<br>",
    "Health Condition: ", health_by_borough$animal_condition, "<br>",
    "Count: ", health_by_borough$n
  )

# Create stacked bar chart using plotly with custom colors and hover info
plot_ly(
    data  = health_by_borough,
    x     = ~borough,
    y     = ~n,
    color = ~animal_condition,
    type  = "bar",
    colors = custom_colors,
    text  = ~hover_text,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    height = 600,
    width = 700
  ) |>
  layout(
    title  = "Health Conditions by Borough",
    xaxis  = list(title = "Borough"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Number of Cases"),
    barmode = "stack"
  )
```

Manhattan has the highest overall number of reports, followed by Queens and Brooklyn.  

But once the data are split by health condition, several boroughs show patterns that differ from their overall ranking:  

- Queens has very few Unknown cases, possibly because calls there provide clearer information or responders have better visibility.  

- Staten Island has more DOA cases but fewer Unhealthy ones, likely because the area is less populated—wildlife is less monitored, so sick animals are less often noticed, whereas dead animals are more likely to be found.  

- Manhattan shows slightly fewer Injured cases, which may reflect limited wildlife movement in dense urban areas.  

- The Bronx has slightly more Healthy reports, suggesting that encounters there may involve animals that are active and visible rather than distressed.  
These differences highlight how each borough’s environment and reporting behavior shape the types of wildlife cases observed.  

<br><br>

# Inferential and Associational Analysis

### Chi-Square Test: relation between species status and animal condition

```{r}
# conduct a chi-square test on species_status and animal_condition
spec_health_tbl = table(park_ranger_new$species_status, park_ranger_new$animal_condition)

spec_health_result = chisq.test(spec_health_tbl)

# show contingency table of the chi-square test
kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(spec_health_result$observed),
  caption = "Observed Counts for Species Status and Animal Condition",
  digits = 2
)

# show result tables of the chi-square test
kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(spec_health_result$expected),
  caption = "Expected Counts for Species Status and Animal Condition",
  digits = 2
)
```


```{r}
# create custom color gradient with more detailed breaks
chi_squre_color_breaks = c(-Inf, -20, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 20)
chi_squre_palette = c("#08306B", "#2171B5", "#6BAED6", "#DEEBF7", "#FEE5D9", "#FB6A4A","#A50F15")
```


```{r}
# plot the standardized residual from the chi-square test between species_status and animal_condition
res_heatmap = as.data.frame(spec_health_result$stdres) |>
  rename(
    species_status = Var1,
    animal_condition = Var2,
    stdres = Freq
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = animal_condition, y = species_status, fill = stdres)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colors = chi_squre_palette,
    values = rescale(chi_squre_color_breaks),
    breaks = chi_squre_color_breaks,
    limits = c(-22, 22),
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 30,
      barheight = 0.8,
      direction = "horizontal",
      title.position = "top"
    ), 
    name = paste0("Std. Residual\nBlue = Obs < Exp", strrep(" ", 116), "Red = Obs > Exp")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(stdres, 2)), size = 3, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Standardized Residuals for Species Status and Animal Condition",
    x = "Animal Condition",
    y = "Species Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9, vjust = 4, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )

plot(res_heatmap)

```

A chi-square test of independence was conducted to evaluate the association between species status and animal condition. The test produced a highly significant result, $$\chi^2(16) = 757.19,\quad p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$$ indicating that the distribution of animal conditions differs substantially across species status categories.

The tables of observed and expected counts are shown above, along with the plot of standardized residuals for the two variables. Based on both the contingency table and the residual plot, domestic species are noticeably overrepresented in the Healthy category, while native (non-domestic) species are underrepresented. Domestic species are also underrepresented in the Injured category, whereas native species show the opposite pattern, with more Injured or Unhealthy cases than expected.

One possible explanation is reporting behavior. Domestic animals may be reported for a wider range of reasons, such as being lost, found unattended, or involved in non-medical encounters, which increases the number of Healthy reports. In contrast, native wildlife is more likely to be reported only when something is wrong, such as being injured, sick, or otherwise in distress, leading to higher counts in those categories.

# Spatial Analysis of Animal Health Conditions Across Boroughs

```{r, include=FALSE}
# import borough dataset
boro_bound_df = read_csv("data/Borough_Boundaries_20251107.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()
```


```{r}
#create a dataframe for plotting
# get all animal classes
animal_classes = c(
  "Birds / Raptors", 
  "Small Mammals", 
  "Large Mammals",
  "Marine Mammals", 
  "Reptiles / Amphibians",
  "Fish", 
  "Others")

# select a subset of park ranger data, and only keep Unhealthy and Injured cases
# group by borough and animal class
# get the number of cases for each animal class in each borough
# get total number of cases for each borough
# join the multipolygon geometry into this dataset
map_boro = park_ranger_new |> 
  select(borough, animal_class_new, animal_condition) |> 
  group_by(borough, animal_class_new) |> 
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = animal_class_new,
    values_from = n) |> 
  mutate(
    total_n = rowSums(across(all_of(animal_classes)), na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  left_join(boro_bound_df |> select(boro_name, the_geom),
            by = c("borough" = "boro_name"))
```

### Map out the total number of cases in borough


```{r}
# create custom color gradient for each borough
map_boro_palette = c(
  "#f0f9e8",
  "#bae4bc",
  "#7bccc4",
  "#43a2ca",
  "#0868ac"
)

map_boro_palette_2 = c(
  "#f7fcf5",  
  "#f0f9e8",
  "#bae4bc",
  "#7bccc4",
  "#43a2ca",
  "#0868ac",
  "#084081"  
)
```


```{r}
# for each borough, create a dataframe for number of cases (>0) for each animal class

# plot the case number for each borough, and saved in tmpfile to present in the map popup window
# convert WKT multipolygon strings into sf multipolygon geometry for mapping
map_boro_sf = map_boro |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    case_num = list(c_across(all_of(animal_classes))),
    map_boro_plot_df = list(tibble(
      class = animal_classes,
      number = unlist(case_num)) |> 
        filter(!is.na(number))),
    map_boro_plot = {
      boro_plot = ggplot(map_boro_plot_df, aes(x = reorder(class, -number), y = number)) +
        geom_col(fill = "#74c476") +
        geom_text(aes(label = number), 
            vjust = -0.3, 
            size = 3) +
        scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
          axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          plot.margin = margin(5,5,5,5)) +
        labs(x = NULL, y = "Case Number")
      tmpfile = tempfile(fileext = ".png")
      ggsave(tmpfile, boro_plot, width = 4, height = 3, dpi = 150)
      dataURI(file = tmpfile)
    },
    popup_content = paste0(
      "<b>", borough, "</b><br>",
      "<img src='", map_boro_plot, "' width='260px'>")) |>
  ungroup() |> 
  arrange(total_n) |>
  mutate(color_hex = map_boro_palette[row_number()]) |> 
  st_as_sf(wkt = "the_geom", crs = 4326)
```



```{r}
# create map of borough with leaflet

# use CartoDB.Voyager tile layer
# fill in color using density_color based on total_n
# add a minimap
leaflet(map_boro_sf) |> 
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Voyager") |>
  addPolygons(
    color = "#238b45",
    weight = 0.8,
    opacity = 0.8,
    fillColor = ~color_hex,
    fillOpacity = 0.5,
    popup = ~popup_content
  ) %>%
  addMiniMap(toggleDisplay = TRUE)
```
  
<br><br>

### Bar plot for borough

```{r, fig.height=6}
# pivot to long format for plotting
# factor relevel borough and animal class
map_boro |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(animal_classes),
    names_to = "animal_class",
    values_to = "cases") |> 
  filter(!is.na(cases) & cases > 0) |> 
  mutate(
    borough = factor(borough,
      levels = map_boro |> arrange(desc(total_n)) |> pull(borough)),
    animal_class = factor(animal_class, levels = animal_classes)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = cases, fill = animal_class)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = map_boro_palette_2,
    name   = "Animal Class"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Borough",
    y = "Number of Cases",
    title = "Number of Reported Cases by Borough"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

The map displays the number of reported cases for each animal class within the selected borough. To map these cases spatially, we used the **Borough Boundaries** dataset released by the Department of City Planning (DCP) on NYC OpenData[https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Borough-Boundaries/gthc-hcne/about_data]. Darker shading represents boroughs with a higher total number of reported cases. Based on the visualization, Manhattan shows the highest number of reported cases overall. 

The accompanying bar plot provides a clearer comparison across boroughs. Manhattan has the highest total number of cases, driven largely by small mammals. Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn all report particularly high counts for birds/raptors, whereas Staten Island shows the highest numbers for marine mammals, fish, and reptiles/amphibians, and the Bronx reports the highest number of cases involving large mammals.

These patterns may be influenced by differences in human population density and land use. Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn have denser human activity, which may increase both encounter rates and incident reporting, especially for small mammals. Human activities in Staten Island often take place near coastal or aquatic environments, making marine animals and other water-dependent species more visible to the public. The Bronx includes the Bronx Zoo and several large parks, which may contribute to a greater presence of large mammals.

Based on these observations, the Parks and Recreation Department could consider allocating more aquatic-animal expertise to Staten Island and strengthening monitoring capacity for its land areas. Additional resources could also be directed toward managing large mammals in the Bronx and reducing human–wildlife disturbances involving small mammals in Manhattan.
